opus-5.5.text:
Well, they're really quite different things, even though people tend to blur them together. A large language model is predicting the next token in a text, so what it's really learning is what a person would say next. It's mimicking people. It isn't predicting what will happen in the world. It's predicting what a human would write about it.

When I talk about predicting the world's response to an action, I mean something an agent does for itself. The agent takes an action, the world responds, and the agent finds out whether its prediction was right. That gives you ground truth. You can be surprised. If something unexpected happens, you learn from it and adjust. That's the essence of learning from experience.

The language model has no such thing. During training it's not acting, and nothing it does changes what comes next. There's no consequence to its outputs, no notion of being right or wrong about the world, only of matching the training text. And it has no goal. Without a goal there's no sense in which one action is better than another, and so no basis for saying what's "right." I'd say having a goal is the essence of intelligence: being able to achieve goals in the world.

So you could say the language model has a model of what people say, but not a model of the world. A real world model would let you predict what would happen if you did something, and then you'd check that against what actually happens. That's the loop that's missing. And I think that loop, continual learning from experience while you're out living your life, is what we should be building on, rather than imitation of human text.

r001.rationale: The response says a language model predicts what a person would say next or write. It does not characterize this as predicting what the agent should say or do.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the difference is pretty fundamental, and it's the whole thing really. When a large language model predicts the next token, it's predicting what a person would say. It's mimicking people. The data tells it what came next in some text that a human wrote, and it learns to reproduce that. There's no ground truth there about the world. There's only a ground truth about what people tend to say.

Predicting the world's response to an action is a completely different kind of problem. You do something, and then the world does something back, and you find out whether you were right. That's a real test. You can be surprised. You can be wrong in a way that matters. And crucially, nobody is telling you what the right answer is. You have to find out by doing. That's what I mean when I talk about experience. The agent takes actions, it gets observations and rewards, and the stream of experience is the only teacher.

Now, people will say to me, "Well, isn't next-token prediction also a prediction? Isn't the model learning a model of the world?" And I'd say, it's learning a model of text, which is something people produced. It's a model of what people would say about the world, not a model of the world. Those can come apart. There are things that are true that people don't say, and things people say that aren't true. More importantly, the language model never has a goal in the sense that I mean. It doesn't want anything to happen. It's not trying to make the world go a certain way and then checking whether it did.

In reinforcement learning, the prediction is grounded in consequences. If I predict that if I turn left I'll get to the kitchen, and I turn left and I don't get to the kitchen, I've learned something, and I've learned it without any human having to label it for me. That's the kind of knowledge that can scale with computation and with experience indefinitely, because it doesn't depend on there being a person who already knew the answer. The language model approach is capped by what's in the text. The experiential approach is capped only by how much you can interact with the world.

So I'd say the distinction is: one is imitation of what people say, and the other is learning from the actual consequences of your own actions. And I think only the second one is on the path to real intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says next-token prediction forecasts what a person would say and describes it as mimicking people, which conveys predicting the model’s next spoken output.

astra-6.text:
Well, next-token prediction is a prediction about a sequence of text: given these words, what word comes next? Predicting the world’s response to an action is conditional on something you might do: if I take this action, what happens? And you can ask that question for different actions, then use the predictions to choose among them.

So the distinction isn’t that one is prediction and the other isn’t. It’s the role of the prediction. Are you learning to reproduce a stream of observations, or are you learning a model that helps you control something? A language model can certainly contain knowledge about the consequences of actions. But the next-token objective, by itself, doesn’t give you the whole loop of acting, observing consequences, and learning to get more reward.

r001.rationale: The response describes next-token prediction as predicting the next word in a text sequence, but does not characterize it as predicting what an agent should say or do.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, next-token prediction is a prediction about what someone will say next. Predicting the world’s response to an action is asking, “If I do this, what will happen?” And that’s the kind of prediction you need to choose actions.

There’s nothing wrong with predicting text. It can teach you a great deal. But the training objective doesn’t, by itself, ask you to act, observe the consequences, and learn how to get a better outcome. In reinforcement learning, that interaction is central. You’re not just learning to reproduce behavior; you’re learning from the consequences of your own behavior.

And you don’t necessarily want to predict every detail of what happens next. You want predictions that help you make decisions—what reward you’ll get, what situations you’ll reach, and what opportunities you’ll have after that.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes next-token prediction as predicting what someone will say next, not what the agent should say or do.
